synthesis.tldr: Master core system design concepts in just 54 minutes with clear analogies and interview insights.
keyTakeaways: Understand the Computer Memory Hierarchy: Disk storage (80-3500 MB/s) ↔ RAM (5000+ MB/s) ↔ Cache (nanoseconds).

In just 54 minutes, this comprehensive crash course by freeCodeCamp takes you through every key element of system design, equipping you with the knowledge needed to ace your next interview. The instructor skillfully breaks down complex concepts, from understanding the computer memory hierarchy and production app architecture to navigating advanced topics like the CAP theorem and application layer protocols, using relatable analogies throughout for clarity.

Don't miss exploring the interactive tabs to quiz yourself after each chapter and deepen your understanding of these essential system design principles!

keyPoints.title: Computer memory hierarchy: Disk → RAM → Cache → CPU registers
keyPoints.detail: Disk storage (HDD 80-160 MB/s, SSD 500-3500 MB/s) holds all data persistently. RAM (5000+ MB/s) holds active variables and application data. Cache (nanoseconds, L1/L2/L3) stores frequently accessed data. CPU checks L1 cache first, then L2, L3, then RAM—each level trades size for speed.

keyPoints.title: Production app architecture: CI/CD pipeline → Load balancer → Multiple servers → External storage
keyPoints.detail: CI/CD (Jenkins, GitHub Actions) automates deployment. Load balancers (Nginx) distribute requests across servers. External storage (database) sits on separate network. Logging stored on external services (PM2 backend, Sentry frontend). Alerts push to Slack for instant developer response.

keyPoints.title: CAP theorem: Choose 2 of 3—Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance
keyPoints.detail: Consistency: all nodes have same data simultaneously. Availability: system always operational and responsive. Partition tolerance: system works even when network disruption occurs. Banking systems prioritize Consistency + Partition tolerance (sacrifice Availability). Trade-offs are unavoidable in every design decision.

keyPoints.title: Availability measured in nines: 99.9% = 8.76 hours downtime/year; 99.99% = ~5 minutes/year
keyPoints.detail: SLO (Service Level Objective) sets performance goals, e.g., 300ms response time at 99.9%. SLA (Service Level Agreement) is formal contract with compensation if breached. Higher availability requires redundancy, failover systems, and graceful degradation for core functionality.

keyPoints.title: Throughput vs Latency: RPS (requests/sec), QPS (queries/sec), bytes/sec vs single request response time
keyPoints.detail: Throughput measures system capacity over time; higher RPS/QPS = better performance. Latency measures single-request delay. Batching operations increases throughput but increases latency—these metrics often trade off against each other.

keyPoints.title: IP addressing: IPv4 (32-bit, ~4B addresses) vs IPv6 (128-bit, vastly more addresses)
keyPoints.detail: Each device on network has unique IP address. IP header in each packet contains sender/receiver IP ensuring data reaches correct destination. IPv6 adoption driven by device explosion. Packets also contain IP header with essential routing information.

keyPoints.title: TCP vs UDP: TCP reliable (sequence numbers, three-way handshake) vs UDP fast (no connection, data loss acceptable)
keyPoints.detail: TCP ensures complete and correct packet delivery through sequence tracking and connection establishment. UDP skips connection setup and guarantees nothing, making it ideal for latency-sensitive apps (video calls, live streaming). TCP header carries port numbers and control flags.

keyPoints.title: DNS translates domain names to IP addresses; uses A records (IPv4) and AAAA records (IPv6)
keyPoints.detail: When you enter URL, browser sends DNS query to find IP address. ICANN coordinates IP space globally. Registrars (Namecheap, GoDaddy) accredited by ICANN sell domain names. DNS queries use specific record types to map domains to addresses.

keyPoints.title: Firewalls monitor/control network traffic; ports (80 HTTP, 22 SSH) identify specific services on IP address
keyPoints.detail: Public IP addresses unique across internet; private IPs unique within local network. Dynamic IPs change over time (residential connections); static IPs permanently assigned. IP + Port = unique network service identifier.

keyPoints.title: HTTP: stateless request-response protocol; GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE for CRUD operations
keyPoints.detail: HTTP is built on TCP/IP with no memory between requests—each request contains all necessary info. Status codes: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error. Each request has headers (URL, method) and body (request/response substance).

keyPoints.title: WebSockets: two-way communication over single long-lived connection for real-time updates without repeated HTTP cycles
keyPoints.detail: HTTP is one-way; WebSockets enable bidirectional push from server to client. Essential for chat apps, live sports updates, stock feeds. Avoids overhead of repeated HTTP request-response cycles.

keyPoints.title: Email protocols: SMTP (sending), IMAP (retrieving, multi-device), POP3 (downloading to local client)
keyPoints.detail: SMTP is standard for inter-server email transmission. IMAP allows access and manipulation from multiple devices. POP3 downloads emails to single device. Most email clients use SMTP for sending and IMAP/POP3 for retrieval.

keyPoints.title: FTP for file transfer; SSH for secure remote operations (login, commands, file transfer)
keyPoints.detail: FTP used in website maintenance and large data transfers. SSH operates securely over unsecured networks. Both are traditional protocols for file/command operations between machines.

keyPoints.title: WebRTC enables browser-to-browser real-time comms (voice, video, file share) without plugins; MQTT for IoT (lightweight, low bandwidth)
keyPoints.detail: WebRTC: peer-to-peer voice/video without intermediaries or plugins—essential for video conferencing. MQTT: lightweight protocol for devices with limited power (IoT sensors). AMQP for enterprise messaging (RabbitMQ).

keyPoints.title: RPC (Remote Procedure Call): invoke function on remote machine as if it were local; abstracts network details
keyPoints.detail: Program on one computer executes code on server/another computer seamlessly. HTTP requests can trigger RPC calls on backend. SMTP servers use RPC internally. Allows developer to interact with remote functions transparently.

keyPoints.title: REST API design: CRUD operations via GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE; stateless, JSON data exchange
keyPoints.detail: POST to /api/products with body creates product. GET to /api/products retrieves all, /api/products/{id} retrieves one. PUT/PATCH to /api/products/{id} updates. DELETE to /api/products/{id} removes. Each request is independent.

keyPoints.title: API paradigms: REST (stateless, easy), GraphQL (query exactly what needed, avoids over/under-fetching), gRPC (HTTP/2, protocol buffers, microservices)
keyPoints.detail: REST: standard HTTP methods, JSON, simple but may over/under-fetch. GraphQL: strongly typed, post-only, efficient but complex queries impact server. gRPC: binary (protocol buffers), multiplexing, HTTP/2, less human-readable but efficient for microservices.

keyPoints.title: API relationships and pagination: GET /users/{id}/orders; limit/offset for pagination; filter by date range
keyPoints.detail: Design endpoints reflecting data relationships (user-to-orders, orders-to-products). Pagination using limit/offset prevents overwhelming system. Filtering by start/end dates reduces data retrieval. GET requests must be idempotent—same result every call.

keyPoints.title: API versioning and backward compatibility: /v1/products vs /v2/products; add new fields without removing old ones
keyPoints.detail: REST: introduce version 2 endpoint so version 1 still serves old clients. GraphQL: add new fields without removing old ones. Rate limiting prevents DDoS attacks (control requests per timeframe). CORS settings control which domains access your API.

keyPoints.title: Browser caching: cache-control header sets duration (e.g., 7200 seconds = 2 hours); stored in local cache directory
keyPoints.detail: Browser stores HTML, CSS, JS locally so revisits load faster. Cache hit = data found; cache miss = fetch from server. Cache-control header tells browser how long to cache. Users can disable via browser settings. X-cache header shows hit/miss status.

keyPoints.title: Server-side caching (Redis, Memcache) reduces expensive database queries; check cache before querying database
keyPoints.detail: Server checks in-memory cache (Redis) before querying database. If found, return immediately. If miss, query database, return result to user, store in cache for future requests. Reduces database load and improves response time.

keyPoints.title: Cache write strategies: write-around (bypass cache), write-through (simultaneous cache+disk), write-back (cache first, disk later)
keyPoints.detail: Write-around: skip cache, go straight to storage—less critical writes. Write-through: write to both cache and disk simultaneously—ensures consistency but slower. Write-back: write to cache then disk—fast but risk of data loss on crash.

keyPoints.title: Cache eviction policies when full: LRU (least recently used), FIFO (first in first out), LFU (least frequently used)
keyPoints.detail: When cache is full, these policies determine what to remove. LRU removes items not used recently. FIFO removes oldest items. LFU removes least-accessed items. Helps maintain cache efficiency and available space.

keyPoints.title: CDN (Content Delivery Network): geographically distributed servers serving static assets (JS, CSS, images, videos) from nearest location
keyPoints.detail: Pull-based CDN: automatically caches content from origin when first requested—ideal for frequently updated static content. Push-based CDN: you upload to origin, CDN distributes—ideal for large infrequently-updated files. Reduces latency, adds availability, handles high traffic.

keyPoints.title: Database caching: cache query results to avoid repeated expensive queries on same data
keyPoints.detail: Check cache for query result before hitting database. If found, return cached result. If miss, execute query, store result in cache for future requests. Especially beneficial for read-heavy applications with frequently executed queries.

keyPoints.title: Forward proxies hide client identity; reverse proxies hide server identity
keyPoints.detail: A forward proxy sits between clients and external servers, masking the client's IP address so requests appear to come from the proxy. A reverse proxy sits in front of web servers, intercepting client requests and hiding server details. The speaker uses the analogy: forward proxy = client's shield, reverse proxy = server's shield.

keyPoints.title: Reverse proxies enable load balancing, SSL offloading, and CDN delivery
keyPoints.detail: Reverse proxies distribute traffic across multiple servers, handle encryption/decryption tasks to reduce server load, and can compress data. CDNs are a type of reverse proxy that cache static content geographically closer to users for faster delivery. Web application firewalls positioned in front of applications also use reverse proxy architecture.

keyPoints.title: Round robin, least connections, and IP hashing are core load balancing strategies
keyPoints.detail: Round robin sequentially distributes requests across equal-capacity servers in rotating order. Least connections directs traffic to the server with fewest active connections (better for uneven load). IP hashing maps client IPs to specific servers consistently, essential for session persistence. The speaker explains weighted variants exist when servers have different CPU/RAM capabilities.

keyPoints.title: Consistent hashing distributes data across nodes using a hash ring
keyPoints.detail: Data and nodes are both hashed onto a circular hash ring where the end wraps to the beginning. This ensures clients consistently connect to the same server and handles node addition/removal with minimal data redistribution. The speaker introduces this as an essential load balancing algorithm for distributed systems.

keyPoints.title: Load balancers are a single point of failure — redundancy and failover required
keyPoints.detail: When a load balancer fails, all servers behind it become unavailable to clients. To mitigate: deploy redundant load balancers in pairs (failover), continuously health-check the load balancers themselves, and use auto-scaling to automatically replace failed instances. DNS failover can reroute traffic from a failed load balancer IP to a standby IP.

keyPoints.title: ACID guarantees data integrity; CAP theorem requires choosing two of three properties
keyPoints.detail: ACID = Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (valid state after transaction), Isolation (independent transactions), Durability (committed data persists). CAP theorem states you can only guarantee two of: Consistency, Availability, or Partition tolerance. The speaker emphasizes interview priority: identify requirements first, then choose which two properties to prioritize.

keyPoints.title: Database sharding splits data across multiple servers; replication copies data for availability
keyPoints.detail: Sharding distributes different data chunks across servers (range-based, directory-based, or geographical). Replication keeps identical copies on multiple servers — master-slave (one read/write master, read-only slaves) or master-master (multiple read/write databases). The speaker clarifies sharding solves scalability; replication solves availability.

keyPoints.title: Database performance gains: caching queries, indexing columns, and query optimization
keyPoints.detail: Use in-memory databases like Redis to cache frequent queries. Create indexes on frequently accessed columns to dramatically speed retrieval. Optimize queries by minimizing joins and using tools like SQL EXPLAIN PLAN to understand performance bottlenecks. The speaker treats these three techniques as the standard performance toolkit.

concepts.name: Cache
concepts.definition: A smaller, faster temporary storage that holds a copy of frequently used data. Access times are nanoseconds (L1 CPU cache) compared to milliseconds for RAM. Purpose is to reduce average time to access data by storing it closer to the processor.
concepts.example: CPU checks L1 cache (few nanoseconds) before checking L2, L3 cache, then RAM (microseconds). Browser cache stores website resources locally so revisits load from local cache rather than network.
concepts.analogy: Like keeping a desk in front of you (cache) for frequent items instead of walking to a filing cabinet (RAM) each time you need something.

concepts.name: CAP Theorem
concepts.definition: Brewers theorem stating distributed systems can achieve only 2 of 3 properties: Consistency (all nodes same data), Availability (always operational), Partition tolerance (works during network disruptions). Every system must trade off one property.
concepts.example: Banking systems choose Consistency + Partition tolerance (sacrifice Availability)—transactions may take longer to ensure accuracy. Social media may choose Availability + Partition tolerance (sacrifice Consistency)—likes may not update instantly everywhere.

concepts.name: Consistency
concepts.definition: All nodes in a distributed system have the same data at the same time. When data changes on one node, that change is immediately reflected across all nodes.
concepts.example: Updating a Google Doc—one person edits, everyone else sees the edit immediately. Banking system transfer—money leaves one account, appears in another atomically.

concepts.name: Availability
concepts.definition: System is always operational and responsive to requests. Measured in nines (99.9%, 99.99%). Allows for specific downtime budget per year.
concepts.example: 99.9% availability = 8.76 hours downtime/year. 99.99% availability = ~5 minutes downtime/year. Online store must always be open to accept orders regardless of backend issues.

concepts.name: Partition Tolerance
concepts.definition: System continues functioning even when network partitions occur—disruptions in communication between nodes. System doesn't crash when nodes can't talk to each other.
concepts.example: Group chat continues if one person loses connection—rest of group can keep messaging. Distributed database continues serving some requests even if some nodes are unreachable.

concepts.name: SLO (Service Level Objective)
concepts.definition: Internal performance goal for system reliability and availability. Sets target metrics like response time or uptime percentage that engineering team aims for.
concepts.example: SLO: web service responds within 300ms at 99.9% of requests. SLO: database processes queries within 50ms at 99.99% of time.

concepts.name: SLA (Service Level Agreement)
concepts.definition: Formal contract between service provider and customer defining minimum service level commitment. If breached, compensation (refunds, credits) is provided.
concepts.example: SLA: 99.99% availability. If actual availability drops below 99.99%, company provides refund or service credits to customers.

concepts.name: Throughput
concepts.definition: Amount of data system can handle over a period of time. Measured in requests/sec (RPS), queries/sec (QPS), or bytes/sec. Higher values indicate better capacity.
concepts.example: Server throughput: 10,000 RPS = handles 10,000 requests per second. Database throughput: 5,000 QPS = processes 5,000 queries per second. Network throughput: 1 GB/s.

concepts.name: Latency
concepts.definition: Time it takes for a single request to receive a response. Measured in milliseconds or microseconds. Latency and throughput often trade off.
concepts.example: Request sent at 0ms, response received at 150ms = 150ms latency. Batching operations increases throughput but increases latency.

concepts.name: IP Address
concepts.definition: Unique identifier for each device on a network. IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses (~4 billion unique), IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses (vastly more). Enables data packets to reach correct destination.
concepts.example: IPv4: 192.168.1.1. IPv6: 2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334. Each device on internet has unique public IP.

concepts.name: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)
concepts.definition: Transport layer protocol ensuring reliable communication. Guarantees complete and correct delivery through sequence numbers and three-way handshake. Connection-oriented.
concepts.example: Web browsing (HTTP over TCP), email (SMTP over TCP). TCP header includes port numbers, sequence numbers, and control flags. Establishes connection before sending data.
concepts.analogy: Like a delivery person checking that package arrives intact and in correct order.

concepts.name: UDP (User Datagram Protocol)
concepts.definition: Transport layer protocol prioritizing speed over reliability. No connection setup, no guaranteed delivery or ordering. Acceptable data loss for latency-sensitive apps.
concepts.example: Video calls, live streaming, online games—where speed matters more than perfect delivery. Video frames lost briefly are acceptable; connection delay would ruin experience.

concepts.name: DNS (Domain Name System)
concepts.definition: System that translates human-friendly domain names into IP addresses. Acts like internet's phonebook. Uses A records (IPv4) and AAAA records (IPv6).
concepts.example: When you enter google.com, DNS query finds Google's IP address. ICANN coordinates global IP space; registrars (Namecheap, GoDaddy) accredited by ICANN sell domains.

concepts.name: HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol)
concepts.definition: Stateless request-response protocol built on TCP/IP. Each request contains all necessary information; server doesn't store context between requests. Uses standard methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) and status codes.
concepts.example: GET /api/products retrieves products. POST /api/products creates new product. Status 200 = success, 404 = not found, 500 = server error. Headers contain URL and method; body contains data.
concepts.analogy: Conversation with no memory—each interaction stands alone with no recollection of past.

concepts.name: WebSocket
concepts.definition: Protocol providing two-way communication over a single long-lived connection. Server can push real-time updates to clients without repeated request-response cycles.
concepts.example: Chat applications (real-time messages), live sports updates, stock market feeds. Single connection stays open; both client and server can send data anytime.

concepts.name: REST (Representational State Transfer)
concepts.definition: API architecture paradigm using stateless HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) for CRUD operations. Each request is independent. Standard, easily consumable by different clients.
concepts.example: POST /products (create), GET /products (read all), PUT /products/{id} (update), DELETE /products/{id} (delete). Uses JSON for data exchange. Simple but may over/under-fetch data.

concepts.name: GraphQL
concepts.definition: Query language for APIs allowing clients to request exactly what data they need. Avoids over-fetching and under-fetching. All requests are POST. Strongly typed but complex queries impact performance.
concepts.example: Client specifies exact fields needed in query. Server returns only requested data, not entire resource. Errors returned with HTTP 200 status but details in response body.

concepts.name: gRPC (Google Remote Procedure Call)
concepts.definition: High-performance RPC framework built on HTTP/2. Uses protocol buffers for serialization (binary, efficient). Supports multiplexing and server push. Ideal for microservices.
concepts.example: Microservice-to-microservice communication. Protocol buffers serialize structured data efficiently. Less human-readable than JSON but requires less bandwidth. Needs HTTP/2 support.

concepts.name: RPC (Remote Procedure Call)
concepts.definition: Protocol allowing program on one computer to execute code on server or another computer. Abstracts network details; developer invokes function as if it were local.
concepts.example: HTTP requests trigger RPC calls on backend. SMTP servers use RPC internally. Seamlessly interact with remote functions; network complexity hidden.

concepts.name: Browser caching
concepts.definition: Storing website resources (HTML, CSS, JS) on user's local computer. Browser serves from cache on revisits, avoiding network fetch. Controlled by cache-control header.
concepts.example: Cache-control: 7200 (cache for 2 hours). Browser stores in local cache directory. Cache hit = served from cache; cache miss = fetch from server. Users can disable via settings.

concepts.name: Server-side caching
concepts.definition: Storing frequently accessed data on server (Redis, Memcache) to reduce expensive database queries. Server checks cache before querying database.
concepts.example: Check Redis cache for user data before querying database. If found, return immediately (cache hit). If miss, query database, return to user, store in cache. Reduces database load.

concepts.name: Cache eviction policies
concepts.definition: Rules determining which items to remove when cache is full. Common policies: LRU (least recently used), FIFO (first in first out), LFU (least frequently used).
concepts.example: LRU removes items not accessed recently. FIFO removes oldest items. LFU removes least-accessed items. Maintains cache efficiency and available space.

concepts.name: CDN (Content Delivery Network)
concepts.definition: Geographically distributed network of servers caching and serving static content (JS, CSS, images, videos) from locations nearest to users. Reduces latency and load on origin server.
concepts.example: Pull-based CDN: automatically caches on first request, ideal for frequently updated content. Push-based CDN: you upload to origin, CDN distributes, ideal for infrequently updated large files. User requests redirected to nearest server.

concepts.name: Forward proxy
concepts.definition: A proxy server that sits between clients and external servers, forwarding client requests while masking the client's IP address. The server sees requests coming from the proxy, not the original client. Used for controlling internet access, caching content, and anonymizing requests within internal networks.
concepts.example: Instagram proxies allow marketers to manage multiple accounts without triggering restrictions by appearing as different users from different locations.
concepts.analogy: A trusted friend who carries your mail to the post office so the recipient never sees your address — only your friend's address.

concepts.name: Reverse proxy
concepts.definition: A proxy server that sits in front of web servers and intercepts requests from clients before they reach the servers. It hides server identity, distributes load, and can handle encryption, compression, and caching. Clients interact only with the reverse proxy and may not know multiple servers exist behind it.
concepts.example: Nginx and HAProxy act as reverse proxies, distributing HTTP requests across backend servers. AWS Elastic Load Balancer and Azure Load Balancer are cloud-based reverse proxies.
concepts.analogy: A receptionist who stands between visitors and office workers, deciding which desk gets each visitor and shielding the workers from direct exposure.

concepts.name: Load balancer
concepts.definition: A system (hardware, software, or cloud-based) that distributes incoming network traffic across multiple servers to ensure no single server becomes overwhelmed. It increases application capacity and reliability by spreading requests effectively. Continuously health-checks servers to direct traffic only to responsive ones.
concepts.example: F5 Big-IP (hardware), HAProxy and Nginx (software), AWS Elastic Load Balancing, Azure Load Balancer, Google Cloud Load Balancer, and Vimeo Advanced Load Balancer (virtual/cloud).
concepts.analogy: A traffic dispatcher at a busy intersection who directs cars to less congested roads to prevent any single road from jamming.

concepts.name: Round robin
concepts.definition: The simplest load balancing algorithm that sequentially distributes requests across servers in rotating order. Each server in the pool gets exactly one request before the cycle repeats. When the last server is reached, the algorithm loops back to the first.
concepts.example: Four servers [A, B, C, D] receive requests 1, 2, 3, 4 as: A→B→C→D→A→B→C→D... The speaker notes this works best when all servers have identical capacity and load is evenly distributed.

concepts.name: Least connections
concepts.definition: A load balancing algorithm that directs each new request to the server with the fewest active connections. Ideal for handling longer-duration tasks or when server load is uneven. More adaptive than round robin because it responds to actual server state.
concepts.example: If Server A has 5 active connections, Server B has 12, and Server C has 3, the next request goes to Server C. Rebalances dynamically as connections complete.

concepts.name: IP hashing
concepts.definition: A load balancing algorithm that determines which server receives a request based on hashing the client's IP address. Ensures the same client always connects to the same server (session persistence). Useful for stateful applications where clients must maintain session context on a specific server.
concepts.example: Client with IP 192.168.1.100 hashes to Server B every time; client 192.168.1.101 hashes to Server A every time. Maintains user state without explicit session tracking.

concepts.name: Consistent hashing
concepts.definition: A hashing algorithm that maps both nodes and data onto a circular hash ring where the end wraps to the beginning. Data is stored on the first node encountered clockwise from its hash position. When nodes are added or removed, only a fraction of data needs remapping, unlike traditional hashing which requires remapping everything.
concepts.example: Imagine 8 servers arranged on a circle at positions 0, 45, 90, 135, 180, 225, 270, 315 degrees. Data hashing to position 100 degrees maps to the server at 135 degrees (next clockwise). If the 90-degree server fails, only data between 45 and 90 degrees rebalances.
concepts.analogy: Like seats at a circular table — when someone leaves, only the people in adjacent seats need to move; the rest stay put. When someone new joins, you insert them in the circle and only nearby people shift.

concepts.name: Health checking
concepts.definition: A load balancer's continuous monitoring process that verifies servers are online and responsive. If a server fails, the load balancer stops directing traffic to it until it recovers. Essential for ensuring requests only reach healthy servers and maintaining service reliability.
concepts.example: A load balancer sends periodic ping requests or health check endpoints to each backend server. If a server doesn't respond within a timeout period, it's marked unhealthy and removed from the pool.

concepts.name: Failover
concepts.definition: An automatic mechanism where a backup system (like a secondary load balancer) takes over when the primary system fails. In redundant load balancing, when one load balancer goes down, another paired load balancer automatically begins handling all traffic.
concepts.example: Two load balancers run in parallel. If LB1 fails, DNS or layer-3 failover automatically reroutes traffic to LB2's standby IP address within seconds. The speaker mentions this is a common approach to avoid load balancer being a single point of failure.

concepts.name: Relational database (SQL)
concepts.definition: A structured database using tables, rows, and columns with predefined schemas. Enforces foreign keys and relationships between tables. Uses SQL query language. ACID-compliant, meaning transactions are Atomic, Consistent, Isolated, and Durable. Strong for complex queries and data integrity but limited horizontal scalability.
concepts.example: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite. The speaker uses the analogy of a 'well-organized filing cabinet with drawers and folders.' Store employee data in one table, departments in another, linked by foreign keys.
concepts.analogy: A filing cabinet with neat drawers and folders — everything has a fixed place, labels are clear, and relationships between folders are explicit.

concepts.name: NoSQL database
concepts.definition: A flexible, schema-less database that does not enforce fixed tables or foreign keys. Often sacrifices consistency (dropping the 'C' from ACID) for scalability and flexibility. Examples include key-value stores (Redis), document databases (MongoDB), and graph databases (Neo4j). Ideal for unstructured data and rapid iteration.
concepts.example: MongoDB stores flexible JSON documents without a fixed schema. Redis stores key-value pairs. Cassandra stores distributed data across many nodes. The speaker describes NoSQL as a 'brainstorming board with sticky notes — add or remove notes in any shape or form.'
concepts.analogy: A brainstorming board with sticky notes in any shape — flexible, easy to rearrange, no fixed structure. Less organized than a filing cabinet but faster to modify.

concepts.name: ACID properties
concepts.definition: Four guarantees for reliable database transactions: **A**tomicity (transaction is all-or-nothing, never partial), **C**onsistency (database moves from one valid state to another), **I**solation (concurrent transactions don't interfere), **D**urability (committed data persists even after system failure). Relational databases enforce ACID; most NoSQL databases relax consistency.
concepts.example: Bank transfer: Debit account A, credit account B. Atomicity ensures both happen or neither happens — never leaving one account debited without the other credited. Durability ensures the committed transfer survives a crash immediately after.

concepts.name: Vertical scaling (scale-up)
concepts.definition: Improving database performance by upgrading a single server's resources: increasing CPU power, adding RAM, upgrading disk storage, or enhancing network bandwidth. Simple to implement but hits a hard limit — there's a maximum amount of resources a single machine can hold.
concepts.example: Your database server runs slow, so you upgrade from 8GB RAM to 64GB RAM, or replace a spinning disk with an SSD. Works until you reach the machine's hardware ceiling.

concepts.name: Horizontal scaling (scale-out)
concepts.definition: Improving database capacity by adding more machines to a cluster rather than upgrading a single machine. Requires distributing data across multiple servers via sharding or replication. Scalable beyond single-machine limits but adds complexity (distributed systems challenges).
concepts.example: Instead of a single 64GB server, add four 16GB servers and distribute data across them using sharding or replication.

concepts.name: Database sharding
concepts.definition: A horizontal scaling technique that splits data into smaller chunks (shards) and distributes them across multiple servers. Each server holds a subset of the data. Different sharding strategies include range-based (by key range), directory-based (lookup table), and geographical (by location).
concepts.example: User database split by ID range: Server A holds users 1-1M, Server B holds 1M-2M, Server C holds 2M-3M. A query for user 500K routes to Server A. Geographical sharding: North America data on US servers, Europe data on EU servers.

concepts.name: Data replication
concepts.definition: A horizontal scaling technique that keeps copies of data on multiple servers for high availability. If one server fails, replicas ensure data survives. Two models: master-slave (one writable master, read-only slaves) and master-master (multiple read-write databases).
concepts.example: Master-slave: Write to primary database, reads spread across three replica servers. If primary fails, failover promotes a slave to primary. Master-master: Two databases both accept reads and writes, synchronizing changes bidirectionally.

concepts.name: Database indexing
concepts.definition: Creating data structures (typically B-trees) on frequently accessed columns to dramatically speed up retrieval times. Trades write-time cost and storage space for much faster read queries. Essential database performance optimization.
concepts.example: Add an index on the 'email' column of a users table. Queries like 'SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ?'  jump from O(n) table scan to O(log n) index lookup.

concepts.name: Query optimization
concepts.definition: Analyzing and refactoring database queries to reduce execution time. Techniques include minimizing joins, using indexes, and leveraging query analysis tools like EXPLAIN PLAN or SQL query analyzer. Complements indexing as a database performance technique.
concepts.example: A slow query joins five tables. Rewrite it using denormalization or stored procedures. Use EXPLAIN PLAN to identify sequential scans that could use indexes. Push filtering down to the database layer rather than in application code.

Design production architecture with CI/CD automation, load balancing, external storage, and external logging/monitoring for resilience.

Measure system with SLO (internal goal) and SLA (customer contract); higher nines = more infrastructure cost.
Balance throughput and latency; batching increases throughput but increases latency—choose based on use case.
Use TCP for reliability (web, email); use UDP for speed (video calls, gaming) when data loss is acceptable.

Layer caching: browser cache (static assets), server cache (database queries via Redis), CDN (static content from geographically distributed servers).

CDN reduces latency for users worldwide; pull-based for frequent updates, push-based for infrequent large files.
Use forward proxies to hide client IP and control internal network access; use reverse proxies to hide servers, balance load, and add security layers.
Choose load balancing algorithm based on server capacity and session requirements: round robin for equal servers, least connections for uneven load, IP hashing for session persistence.
Implement redundant load balancers with automatic failover to prevent load balancer becoming a single point of failure.

learning.keyQuestion: How do you design scalable, reliable systems using proxies, load balancers, and databases without creating single points of failure?
learning.summary: This segment covers three critical system design layers: (1) Proxy servers (forward proxies hide client identity; reverse proxies hide servers and enable load balancing), (2) Load balancers (distribute traffic using round robin, least connections, IP hashing, or consistent hashing; avoid failure via redundancy and failover), and (3) Databases (relational databases provide ACID; NoSQL provides flexibility; CAP theorem requires choosing two of consistency, availability, partition tolerance; scale horizontally via sharding and replication, vertically via resource upgrades; optimize performance with caching, indexing, and query optimization).

quiz.question: What does the CAP theorem state about distributed systems?
options: A system can provide Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance simultaneously.
A system must sacrifice one of Consistency, Availability, or Partition tolerance.
A system is always consistent if the network is reliable.
A system cannot provide availability if it's consistent.
quiz.explanation: The CAP theorem states that a distributed system can provide at most two out of the three guarantees: Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance. This concept is crucial in system design trade-offs.

quiz.question: Which protocol is used for sending emails between servers?
options: IMAP
POP3
SMTP
HTTP
quiz.explanation: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) is the standard for sending emails between servers, as explained towards the end of the video.

quiz.question: What key metric separates throughput from latency?
options: Throughput measures overall capacity; Latency measures individual request delay.
Throughput measures data sent over a network; Latency measures packet loss.
Throughput is a time metric; Latency is a usage volume metric.
Throughput and Latency are the same thing.
quiz.explanation: Throughput is about how much data the system can handle over time (e.g., requests per second), while latency measures the delay in the response to a single request.

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT a factor that contributes to higher system availability?
options: Redundancy
Failover systems
Graceful degradation
Single point of failure components
quiz.explanation: A single point of failure component does not contribute to higher availability; instead, it increases the risk of system downtime.

flashcards.front: What is the importance of cache in memory hierarchy?
flashcards.back: Cache improves performance by storing frequently accessed data closer to the CPU, allowing for faster data retrieval compared to fetching from RAM.
An SLO sets specific performance goals for a service, such as response time thresholds, e.g., 300ms response time at 99.9% availability.

flashcards.front: What is the main advantage of using TCP over UDP?
flashcards.back: TCP provides reliable communication by ensuring that packets are delivered in order and without errors, while UDP is faster but does not guarantee delivery.
DNS translates user-friendly domain names into IP addresses, enabling browsers to locate and connect to websites.

flashcards.front: What is the function of a load balancer?
flashcards.back: A load balancer distributes incoming network traffic across multiple servers to ensure no single server is overwhelmed and to improve responsiveness.

flashcards.front: Explain how WebSockets differ from HTTP.
flashcards.back: WebSockets enable two-way communication over a single long-lived connection, allowing real-time updates without the overhead of repeated HTTP request-response cycles.

flashcards.front: What are the main HTTP methods used in RESTful APIs?
flashcards.back: Common HTTP methods include GET for retrieving resources, POST for creating resources, PUT/PATCH for updating, and DELETE for removing resources.
Consistent hashing is a strategy for distributing data across a number of nodes in a way that minimizes the reorganization of the data when nodes are added or removed.

flashcards.front: What is meant by 'lazily loaded' data?
flashcards.back: Lazily loaded data refers to a programming technique where data is only retrieved when it is needed, rather than all at once, which can optimize performance and resource use.

flashcards.front: What does the acronym API stand for?
flashcards.back: API stands for Application Programming Interface, which allows different software entities to communicate with each other.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between SLA and SLO?
flashcards.back: An SLA (Service Level Agreement) is a formal contract that defines service expectations and consequences for breaches, while an SLO is an internal performance target that the service aims to meet.

flashcards.front: What characterizes GraphQL compared to REST?
flashcards.back: GraphQL allows clients to request exactly the data they need in a single query, avoiding over-fetching and under-fetching issues typical in REST APIs.
Browser caching uses cache-control headers to specify how long web resources should be stored in the cache, reducing server requests and improving load times.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of firewalls in networking?
flashcards.back: Firewalls monitor and control incoming and outgoing network traffic, helping protect systems from unauthorized access or data breaches.

scenarios.question: You need to design a system that requires high availability for a critical financial application. Which approach is best?

options.text: Utilize a single main server for simplicity.
options.explanation: Using a single server increases the risk of downtime. High availability requires multiple servers and redundancy.

options.text: Implement a load balancer distributing requests across multiple servers.
options.explanation: A load balancer helps distribute the traffic intelligently, which improves system resilience and availability.

options.text: Only rely on frequent backups to prevent data loss.
options.explanation: Frequent backups do not prevent downtime; they are useful for data recovery, but do not provide active fault tolerance.

options.text: Use a single point of failure design only for cost efficiency.
options.explanation: Single points of failure can compromise the system's availability; it's essential to design for redundancy.

scenarios.question: As a web developer, you're tasked with optimizing the performance of a data-heavy application. What strategy should you employ?

options.text: Use only synchronous requests to retrieve data.
options.explanation: Synchronous requests can block processes and reduce performance; asynchronous or batched data fetching improves responsiveness.

options.text: Implement caching strategies to store frequently accessed data.
options.explanation: Caching strategies save frequently used data closer to the application, enhancing speed and performance while reducing database load.

options.text: Ignore API performance metrics since they don't affect the application.
options.explanation: Performance metrics are critical to understanding and optimizing the responsiveness and efficiency of an application.

options.text: Build all components without any scalability considerations.
options.explanation: Ignoring scalability could lead to performance issues as the user base grows; it's important to design with future growth in mind.

scenarios.question: Your company is evaluating whether to switch from a REST API to GraphQL. What is a key benefit of using GraphQL?

options.text: GraphQL is always simpler to implement than REST.
options.explanation: While GraphQL can be efficient for data retrieval, it may involve more complexity in setup compared to REST APIs.

options.text: GraphQL avoids over-fetching and under-fetching of data.
options.explanation: One of the significant advantages of GraphQL is that clients can request only the data they need, optimizing performance.

options.text: REST provides real-time data updates via WebSockets.
options.explanation: REST does not natively support real-time communication; GraphQL can be enhanced with subscriptions for real-time data.

options.text: All GraphQL queries must be made through static endpoints.
options.explanation: GraphQL allows dynamic queries that can fetch data based on client needs instead of fixed endpoints.

scenarios.question: You're monitoring your application's performance metrics and notice high latency with low throughput. What could be a potential cause?

options.explanation: Efficiency in database queries typically contributes to low latency, not the opposite.

options.text: Too many operations being batched together.
options.explanation: Batching operations can improve throughput but may increase latency for individual requests if not managed well.
A fast network connection usually improves both throughput and latency; it should not lead to high latency.
Multiple load balancers are meant to improve performance by distributing traffic, not negatively impacting latency.

tabs.label: 25 Core Concepts

concepts.name: Cache
concepts.definition: A smaller, faster temporary storage that holds a copy of frequently used data. Access times are nanoseconds (L1 CPU cache) compared to milliseconds for RAM. Purpose is to reduce average time to access data by storing it closer to the processor.
concepts.example: CPU checks L1 cache (few nanoseconds) before checking L2, L3 cache, then RAM (microseconds). Browser cache stores website resources locally so revisits load from local cache rather than network.
concepts.analogy: Like keeping a desk in front of you (cache) for frequent items instead of walking to a filing cabinet (RAM) each time you need something.

concepts.name: CAP Theorem
concepts.definition: Brewers theorem stating distributed systems can achieve only 2 of 3 properties: Consistency (all nodes same data), Availability (always operational), Partition tolerance (works during network disruptions). Every system must trade off one property.
concepts.example: Banking systems choose Consistency + Partition tolerance (sacrifice Availability)—transactions may take longer to ensure accuracy. Social media may choose Availability + Partition tolerance (sacrifice Consistency)—likes may not update instantly everywhere.

concepts.name: Consistency
concepts.definition: All nodes in a distributed system have the same data at the same time. When data changes on one node, that change is immediately reflected across all nodes.
concepts.example: Updating a Google Doc—one person edits, everyone else sees the edit immediately. Banking system transfer—money leaves one account, appears in another atomically.

concepts.name: Availability
concepts.definition: System is always operational and responsive to requests. Measured in nines (99.9%, 99.99%). Allows for specific downtime budget per year.
concepts.example: 99.9% availability = 8.76 hours downtime/year. 99.99% availability = ~5 minutes downtime/year. Online store must always be open to accept orders regardless of backend issues.

concepts.name: Partition Tolerance
concepts.definition: System continues functioning even when network partitions occur—disruptions in communication between nodes. System doesn't crash when nodes can't talk to each other.
concepts.example: Group chat continues if one person loses connection—rest of group can keep messaging. Distributed database continues serving some requests even if some nodes are unreachable.

concepts.name: SLO (Service Level Objective)
concepts.definition: Internal performance goal for system reliability and availability. Sets target metrics like response time or uptime percentage that engineering team aims for.
concepts.example: SLO: web service responds within 300ms at 99.9% of requests. SLO: database processes queries within 50ms at 99.99% of time.

concepts.name: SLA (Service Level Agreement)
concepts.definition: Formal contract between service provider and customer defining minimum service level commitment. If breached, compensation (refunds, credits) is provided.
concepts.example: SLA: 99.99% availability. If actual availability drops below 99.99%, company provides refund or service credits to customers.

concepts.name: Throughput
concepts.definition: Amount of data system can handle over a period of time. Measured in requests/sec (RPS), queries/sec (QPS), or bytes/sec. Higher values indicate better capacity.
concepts.example: Server throughput: 10,000 RPS = handles 10,000 requests per second. Database throughput: 5,000 QPS = processes 5,000 queries per second. Network throughput: 1 GB/s.

concepts.name: Latency
concepts.definition: Time it takes for a single request to receive a response. Measured in milliseconds or microseconds. Latency and throughput often trade off.
concepts.example: Request sent at 0ms, response received at 150ms = 150ms latency. Batching operations increases throughput but increases latency.

concepts.name: IP Address
concepts.definition: Unique identifier for each device on a network. IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses (~4 billion unique), IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses (vastly more). Enables data packets to reach correct destination.
concepts.example: IPv4: 192.168.1.1. IPv6: 2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334. Each device on internet has unique public IP.

concepts.name: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)
concepts.definition: Transport layer protocol ensuring reliable communication. Guarantees complete and correct delivery through sequence numbers and three-way handshake. Connection-oriented.
concepts.example: Web browsing (HTTP over TCP), email (SMTP over TCP). TCP header includes port numbers, sequence numbers, and control flags. Establishes connection before sending data.
concepts.analogy: Like a delivery person checking that package arrives intact and in correct order.

concepts.name: UDP (User Datagram Protocol)
concepts.definition: Transport layer protocol prioritizing speed over reliability. No connection setup, no guaranteed delivery or ordering. Acceptable data loss for latency-sensitive apps.
concepts.example: Video calls, live streaming, online games—where speed matters more than perfect delivery. Video frames lost briefly are acceptable; connection delay would ruin experience.

concepts.name: DNS (Domain Name System)
concepts.definition: System that translates human-friendly domain names into IP addresses. Acts like internet's phonebook. Uses A records (IPv4) and AAAA records (IPv6).
concepts.example: When you enter google.com, DNS query finds Google's IP address. ICANN coordinates global IP space; registrars (Namecheap, GoDaddy) accredited by ICANN sell domains.

concepts.name: HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol)
concepts.definition: Stateless request-response protocol built on TCP/IP. Each request contains all necessary information; server doesn't store context between requests. Uses standard methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) and status codes.
concepts.example: GET /api/products retrieves products. POST /api/products creates new product. Status 200 = success, 404 = not found, 500 = server error. Headers contain URL and method; body contains data.
concepts.analogy: Conversation with no memory—each interaction stands alone with no recollection of past.

concepts.name: WebSocket
concepts.definition: Protocol providing two-way communication over a single long-lived connection. Server can push real-time updates to clients without repeated request-response cycles.
concepts.example: Chat applications (real-time messages), live sports updates, stock market feeds. Single connection stays open; both client and server can send data anytime.

concepts.name: REST (Representational State Transfer)
concepts.definition: API architecture paradigm using stateless HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) for CRUD operations. Each request is independent. Standard, easily consumable by different clients.
concepts.example: POST /products (create), GET /products (read all), PUT /products/{id} (update), DELETE /products/{id} (delete). Uses JSON for data exchange. Simple but may over/under-fetch data.

concepts.name: GraphQL
concepts.definition: Query language for APIs allowing clients to request exactly what data they need. Avoids over-fetching and under-fetching. All requests are POST. Strongly typed but complex queries impact performance.
concepts.example: Client specifies exact fields needed in query. Server returns only requested data, not entire resource. Errors returned with HTTP 200 status but details in response body.

concepts.name: gRPC (Google Remote Procedure Call)
concepts.definition: High-performance RPC framework built on HTTP/2. Uses protocol buffers for serialization (binary, efficient). Supports multiplexing and server push. Ideal for microservices.
concepts.example: Microservice-to-microservice communication. Protocol buffers serialize structured data efficiently. Less human-readable than JSON but requires less bandwidth. Needs HTTP/2 support.

concepts.name: RPC (Remote Procedure Call)
concepts.definition: Protocol allowing program on one computer to execute code on server or another computer. Abstracts network details; developer invokes function as if it were local.
concepts.example: HTTP requests trigger RPC calls on backend. SMTP servers use RPC internally. Seamlessly interact with remote functions; network complexity hidden.

concepts.name: Browser caching
concepts.definition: Storing website resources (HTML, CSS, JS) on user's local computer. Browser serves from cache on revisits, avoiding network fetch. Controlled by cache-control header.
concepts.example: Cache-control: 7200 (cache for 2 hours). Browser stores in local cache directory. Cache hit = served from cache; cache miss = fetch from server. Users can disable via settings.

concepts.name: Server-side caching
concepts.definition: Storing frequently accessed data on server (Redis, Memcache) to reduce expensive database queries. Server checks cache before querying database.
concepts.example: Check Redis cache for user data before querying database. If found, return immediately (cache hit). If miss, query database, return to user, store in cache. Reduces database load.

concepts.name: Cache eviction policies
concepts.definition: Rules determining which items to remove when cache is full. Common policies: LRU (least recently used), FIFO (first in first out), LFU (least frequently used).
concepts.example: LRU removes items not accessed recently. FIFO removes oldest items. LFU removes least-accessed items. Maintains cache efficiency and available space.

concepts.name: CDN (Content Delivery Network)
concepts.definition: Geographically distributed network of servers caching and serving static content (JS, CSS, images, videos) from locations nearest to users. Reduces latency and load on origin server.
concepts.example: Pull-based CDN: automatically caches on first request, ideal for frequently updated content. Push-based CDN: you upload to origin, CDN distributes, ideal for infrequently updated large files. User requests redirected to nearest server.

concepts.name: Forward proxy
concepts.definition: A proxy server that sits between clients and external servers, forwarding client requests while masking the client's IP address. The server sees requests coming from the proxy, not the original client. Used for controlling internet access, caching content, and anonymizing requests within internal networks.
concepts.example: Instagram proxies allow marketers to manage multiple accounts without triggering restrictions by appearing as different users from different locations.
concepts.analogy: A trusted friend who carries your mail to the post office so the recipient never sees your address — only your friend's address.

concepts.name: Reverse proxy
concepts.definition: A proxy server that sits in front of web servers and intercepts requests from clients before they reach the servers. It hides server identity, distributes load, and can handle encryption, compression, and caching. Clients interact only with the reverse proxy and may not know multiple servers exist behind it.
concepts.example: Nginx and HAProxy act as reverse proxies, distributing HTTP requests across backend servers. AWS Elastic Load Balancer and Azure Load Balancer are cloud-based reverse proxies.
concepts.analogy: A receptionist who stands between visitors and office workers, deciding which desk gets each visitor and shielding the workers from direct exposure.

concepts.name: Load balancer
concepts.definition: A system (hardware, software, or cloud-based) that distributes incoming network traffic across multiple servers to ensure no single server becomes overwhelmed. It increases application capacity and reliability by spreading requests effectively. Continuously health-checks servers to direct traffic only to responsive ones.
concepts.example: F5 Big-IP (hardware), HAProxy and Nginx (software), AWS Elastic Load Balancing, Azure Load Balancer, Google Cloud Load Balancer, and Vimeo Advanced Load Balancer (virtual/cloud).
concepts.analogy: A traffic dispatcher at a busy intersection who directs cars to less congested roads to prevent any single road from jamming.

concepts.name: Round robin
concepts.definition: The simplest load balancing algorithm that sequentially distributes requests across servers in rotating order. Each server in the pool gets exactly one request before the cycle repeats. When the last server is reached, the algorithm loops back to the first.
concepts.example: Four servers [A, B, C, D] receive requests 1, 2, 3, 4 as: A→B→C→D→A→B→C→D... The speaker notes this works best when all servers have identical capacity and load is evenly distributed.

concepts.name: Least connections
concepts.definition: A load balancing algorithm that directs each new request to the server with the fewest active connections. Ideal for handling longer-duration tasks or when server load is uneven. More adaptive than round robin because it responds to actual server state.
concepts.example: If Server A has 5 active connections, Server B has 12, and Server C has 3, the next request goes to Server C. Rebalances dynamically as connections complete.

concepts.name: IP hashing
concepts.definition: A load balancing algorithm that determines which server receives a request based on hashing the client's IP address. Ensures the same client always connects to the same server (session persistence). Useful for stateful applications where clients must maintain session context on a specific server.
concepts.example: Client with IP 192.168.1.100 hashes to Server B every time; client 192.168.1.101 hashes to Server A every time. Maintains user state without explicit session tracking.

concepts.name: Consistent hashing
concepts.definition: A hashing algorithm that maps both nodes and data onto a circular hash ring where the end wraps to the beginning. Data is stored on the first node encountered clockwise from its hash position. When nodes are added or removed, only a fraction of data needs remapping, unlike traditional hashing which requires remapping everything.

concepts.analogy: Like seats at a circular table — when someone leaves, only the people in adjacent seats need to move; the rest stay put. When someone new joins, you insert them in the circle and only nearby people shift.

concepts.name: Health checking
concepts.definition: A load balancer's continuous monitoring process that verifies servers are online and responsive. If a server fails, the load balancer stops directing traffic to it until it recovers. Essential for ensuring requests only reach healthy servers and maintaining service reliability.
concepts.example: A load balancer sends periodic ping requests or health check endpoints to each backend server. If a server doesn't respond within a timeout period, it's marked unhealthy and removed from the pool.

concepts.name: Failover
concepts.definition: An automatic mechanism where a backup system (like a secondary load balancer) takes over when the primary system fails. In redundant load balancing, when one load balancer goes down, another paired load balancer automatically begins handling all traffic.
concepts.example: Two load balancers run in parallel. If LB1 fails, DNS or layer-3 failover automatically reroutes traffic to LB2's standby IP address within seconds. The speaker mentions this is a common approach to avoid load balancer being a single point of failure.

concepts.name: Relational database (SQL)
concepts.definition: A structured database using tables, rows, and columns with predefined schemas. Enforces foreign keys and relationships between tables. Uses SQL query language. ACID-compliant, meaning transactions are Atomic, Consistent, Isolated, and Durable. Strong for complex queries and data integrity but limited horizontal scalability.
concepts.example: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite. The speaker uses the analogy of a 'well-organized filing cabinet with drawers and folders.' Store employee data in one table, departments in another, linked by foreign keys.
concepts.analogy: A filing cabinet with neat drawers and folders — everything has a fixed place, labels are clear, and relationships between folders are explicit.

concepts.name: NoSQL database
concepts.definition: A flexible, schema-less database that does not enforce fixed tables or foreign keys. Often sacrifices consistency (dropping the 'C' from ACID) for scalability and flexibility. Examples include key-value stores (Redis), document databases (MongoDB), and graph databases (Neo4j). Ideal for unstructured data and rapid iteration.
concepts.example: MongoDB stores flexible JSON documents without a fixed schema. Redis stores key-value pairs. Cassandra stores distributed data across many nodes. The speaker describes NoSQL as a 'brainstorming board with sticky notes — add or remove notes in any shape or form.'
concepts.analogy: A brainstorming board with sticky notes in any shape — flexible, easy to rearrange, no fixed structure. Less organized than a filing cabinet but faster to modify.

concepts.name: ACID properties
concepts.definition: Four guarantees for reliable database transactions: **A**tomicity (transaction is all-or-nothing, never partial), **C**onsistency (database moves from one valid state to another), **I**solation (concurrent transactions don't interfere), **D**urability (committed data persists even after system failure). Relational databases enforce ACID; most NoSQL databases relax consistency.
concepts.example: Bank transfer: Debit account A, credit account B. Atomicity ensures both happen or neither happens — never leaving one account debited without the other credited. Durability ensures the committed transfer survives a crash immediately after.

concepts.name: Vertical scaling (scale-up)
concepts.definition: Improving database performance by upgrading a single server's resources: increasing CPU power, adding RAM, upgrading disk storage, or enhancing network bandwidth. Simple to implement but hits a hard limit — there's a maximum amount of resources a single machine can hold.
concepts.example: Your database server runs slow, so you upgrade from 8GB RAM to 64GB RAM, or replace a spinning disk with an SSD. Works until you reach the machine's hardware ceiling.

concepts.name: Horizontal scaling (scale-out)
concepts.definition: Improving database capacity by adding more machines to a cluster rather than upgrading a single machine. Requires distributing data across multiple servers via sharding or replication. Scalable beyond single-machine limits but adds complexity (distributed systems challenges).
concepts.example: Instead of a single 64GB server, add four 16GB servers and distribute data across them using sharding or replication.

concepts.name: Database sharding
concepts.definition: A horizontal scaling technique that splits data into smaller chunks (shards) and distributes them across multiple servers. Each server holds a subset of the data. Different sharding strategies include range-based (by key range), directory-based (lookup table), and geographical (by location).
concepts.example: User database split by ID range: Server A holds users 1-1M, Server B holds 1M-2M, Server C holds 2M-3M. A query for user 500K routes to Server A. Geographical sharding: North America data on US servers, Europe data on EU servers.

concepts.name: Data replication
concepts.definition: A horizontal scaling technique that keeps copies of data on multiple servers for high availability. If one server fails, replicas ensure data survives. Two models: master-slave (one writable master, read-only slaves) and master-master (multiple read-write databases).
concepts.example: Master-slave: Write to primary database, reads spread across three replica servers. If primary fails, failover promotes a slave to primary. Master-master: Two databases both accept reads and writes, synchronizing changes bidirectionally.

concepts.name: Database indexing
concepts.definition: Creating data structures (typically B-trees) on frequently accessed columns to dramatically speed up retrieval times. Trades write-time cost and storage space for much faster read queries. Essential database performance optimization.
concepts.example: Add an index on the 'email' column of a users table. Queries like 'SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ?'  jump from O(n) table scan to O(log n) index lookup.

concepts.name: Query optimization

questions.question: What does the CAP theorem state about distributed systems?
options: A system can provide Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance simultaneously.
A system must sacrifice one of Consistency, Availability, or Partition tolerance.
A system is always consistent if the network is reliable.
A system cannot provide availability if it's consistent.
questions.explanation: The CAP theorem states that a distributed system can provide at most two out of the three guarantees: Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance. This concept is crucial in system design trade-offs.

questions.question: Which protocol is used for sending emails between servers?
options: IMAP
POP3
SMTP
HTTP
questions.explanation: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) is the standard for sending emails between servers, as explained towards the end of the video.

questions.question: What key metric separates throughput from latency?
options: Throughput measures overall capacity; Latency measures individual request delay.
Throughput measures data sent over a network; Latency measures packet loss.
Throughput is a time metric; Latency is a usage volume metric.
Throughput and Latency are the same thing.
questions.explanation: Throughput is about how much data the system can handle over time (e.g., requests per second), while latency measures the delay in the response to a single request.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a factor that contributes to higher system availability?
options: Redundancy

questions.explanation: A single point of failure component does not contribute to higher availability; instead, it increases the risk of system downtime.

tabs.label: Key Terms

concepts.name: Cache
concepts.definition: A smaller, faster temporary storage that holds a copy of frequently used data. Access times are nanoseconds (L1 CPU cache) compared to milliseconds for RAM. Purpose is to reduce average time to access data by storing it closer to the processor.
concepts.example: CPU checks L1 cache (few nanoseconds) before checking L2, L3 cache, then RAM (microseconds). Browser cache stores website resources locally so revisits load from local cache rather than network.
concepts.analogy: Like keeping a desk in front of you (cache) for frequent items instead of walking to a filing cabinet (RAM) each time you need something.

concepts.name: CAP Theorem
concepts.definition: Brewers theorem stating distributed systems can achieve only 2 of 3 properties: Consistency (all nodes same data), Availability (always operational), Partition tolerance (works during network disruptions). Every system must trade off one property.
concepts.example: Banking systems choose Consistency + Partition tolerance (sacrifice Availability)—transactions may take longer to ensure accuracy. Social media may choose Availability + Partition tolerance (sacrifice Consistency)—likes may not update instantly everywhere.

concepts.name: Consistency
concepts.definition: All nodes in a distributed system have the same data at the same time. When data changes on one node, that change is immediately reflected across all nodes.
concepts.example: Updating a Google Doc—one person edits, everyone else sees the edit immediately. Banking system transfer—money leaves one account, appears in another atomically.

concepts.name: Availability
concepts.definition: System is always operational and responsive to requests. Measured in nines (99.9%, 99.99%). Allows for specific downtime budget per year.
concepts.example: 99.9% availability = 8.76 hours downtime/year. 99.99% availability = ~5 minutes downtime/year. Online store must always be open to accept orders regardless of backend issues.

concepts.name: Partition Tolerance
concepts.definition: System continues functioning even when network partitions occur—disruptions in communication between nodes. System doesn't crash when nodes can't talk to each other.
concepts.example: Group chat continues if one person loses connection—rest of group can keep messaging. Distributed database continues serving some requests even if some nodes are unreachable.

concepts.name: SLO (Service Level Objective)
concepts.definition: Internal performance goal for system reliability and availability. Sets target metrics like response time or uptime percentage that engineering team aims for.
concepts.example: SLO: web service responds within 300ms at 99.9% of requests. SLO: database processes queries within 50ms at 99.99% of time.

concepts.name: SLA (Service Level Agreement)
concepts.definition: Formal contract between service provider and customer defining minimum service level commitment. If breached, compensation (refunds, credits) is provided.
concepts.example: SLA: 99.99% availability. If actual availability drops below 99.99%, company provides refund or service credits to customers.

concepts.name: Throughput
concepts.definition: Amount of data system can handle over a period of time. Measured in requests/sec (RPS), queries/sec (QPS), or bytes/sec. Higher values indicate better capacity.
concepts.example: Server throughput: 10,000 RPS = handles 10,000 requests per second. Database throughput: 5,000 QPS = processes 5,000 queries per second. Network throughput: 1 GB/s.

concepts.name: Latency
concepts.definition: Time it takes for a single request to receive a response. Measured in milliseconds or microseconds. Latency and throughput often trade off.
concepts.example: Request sent at 0ms, response received at 150ms = 150ms latency. Batching operations increases throughput but increases latency.

concepts.name: IP Address
concepts.definition: Unique identifier for each device on a network. IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses (~4 billion unique), IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses (vastly more). Enables data packets to reach correct destination.
concepts.example: IPv4: 192.168.1.1. IPv6: 2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334. Each device on internet has unique public IP.

concepts.name: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)
concepts.definition: Transport layer protocol ensuring reliable communication. Guarantees complete and correct delivery through sequence numbers and three-way handshake. Connection-oriented.
concepts.example: Web browsing (HTTP over TCP), email (SMTP over TCP). TCP header includes port numbers, sequence numbers, and control flags. Establishes connection before sending data.
concepts.analogy: Like a delivery person checking that package arrives intact and in correct order.

concepts.name: UDP (User Datagram Protocol)
concepts.definition: Transport layer protocol prioritizing speed over reliability. No connection setup, no guaranteed delivery or ordering. Acceptable data loss for latency-sensitive apps.
concepts.example: Video calls, live streaming, online games—where speed matters more than perfect delivery. Video frames lost briefly are acceptable; connection delay would ruin experience.

concepts.name: DNS (Domain Name System)
concepts.definition: System that translates human-friendly domain names into IP addresses. Acts like internet's phonebook. Uses A records (IPv4) and AAAA records (IPv6).
concepts.example: When you enter google.com, DNS query finds Google's IP address. ICANN coordinates global IP space; registrars (Namecheap, GoDaddy) accredited by ICANN sell domains.

concepts.name: HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol)
concepts.definition: Stateless request-response protocol built on TCP/IP. Each request contains all necessary information; server doesn't store context between requests. Uses standard methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) and status codes.
concepts.example: GET /api/products retrieves products. POST /api/products creates new product. Status 200 = success, 404 = not found, 500 = server error. Headers contain URL and method; body contains data.
concepts.analogy: Conversation with no memory—each interaction stands alone with no recollection of past.

concepts.name: WebSocket
concepts.definition: Protocol providing two-way communication over a single long-lived connection. Server can push real-time updates to clients without repeated request-response cycles.
concepts.example: Chat applications (real-time messages), live sports updates, stock market feeds. Single connection stays open; both client and server can send data anytime.

concepts.name: REST (Representational State Transfer)
concepts.definition: API architecture paradigm using stateless HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) for CRUD operations. Each request is independent. Standard, easily consumable by different clients.
concepts.example: POST /products (create), GET /products (read all), PUT /products/{id} (update), DELETE /products/{id} (delete). Uses JSON for data exchange. Simple but may over/under-fetch data.

concepts.name: GraphQL
concepts.definition: Query language for APIs allowing clients to request exactly what data they need. Avoids over-fetching and under-fetching. All requests are POST. Strongly typed but complex queries impact performance.
concepts.example: Client specifies exact fields needed in query. Server returns only requested data, not entire resource. Errors returned with HTTP 200 status but details in response body.

concepts.name: gRPC (Google Remote Procedure Call)
concepts.definition: High-performance RPC framework built on HTTP/2. Uses protocol buffers for serialization (binary, efficient). Supports multiplexing and server push. Ideal for microservices.
concepts.example: Microservice-to-microservice communication. Protocol buffers serialize structured data efficiently. Less human-readable than JSON but requires less bandwidth. Needs HTTP/2 support.

concepts.name: RPC (Remote Procedure Call)
concepts.definition: Protocol allowing program on one computer to execute code on server or another computer. Abstracts network details; developer invokes function as if it were local.
concepts.example: HTTP requests trigger RPC calls on backend. SMTP servers use RPC internally. Seamlessly interact with remote functions; network complexity hidden.
